910.name: Lucayan Taíno Civilization
910.description: The Lucayan branch of the Taíno people who settled across the Bahamian archipelago, developing a sophisticated maritime culture, agriculture, and trade networks throughout the islands.

sub_clusters.name: Lucayan Migration and Settlement
sub_clusters.description: Lucayan Taíno peoples migrated northward from Hispaniola and Cuba, settling across the Bahamian archipelago. They established villages, developed agriculture including cassava cultivation, and created extensive inter-island trade networks.

sub_clusters.name: Lucayan Society at Pre-Contact Peak
sub_clusters.description: At their peak, an estimated 30,000–40,000 Lucayans inhabited the Bahamas, organized in chiefdom-level societies. They were skilled seafarers, potters, and agriculturalists who lived in thatched-roof villages.
key_events: Lucayan population reaches estimated 30,000–40,000 across the archipelago
Development of extensive inter-island canoe trade routes

920.name: Columbus Contact and Spanish Depopulation
920.description: Christopher Columbus's first landfall in the New World at San Salvador (Guanahani) in 1492, and the subsequent Spanish enslavement and deportation of the Lucayan population to work in Hispaniola's mines, leading to the complete depopulation of the islands.

sub_clusters.name: Columbus First Landfall at San Salvador
sub_clusters.description: On October 12, 1492, Christopher Columbus made his first landfall in the Americas on the island he named San Salvador (the Lucayan name was Guanahani). This moment marks the beginning of sustained European contact with the New World.
key_events: Columbus lands at San Salvador (Guanahani) on October 12, 1492
First recorded European contact with Lucayan Taíno people

sub_clusters.name: Lucayan Enslavement and Island Depopulation
sub_clusters.description: Spanish slavers systematically captured and deported the Lucayan population to Hispaniola to work in gold mines and on plantations. By 1520, the Bahamas were virtually uninhabited — an estimated 40,000 Lucayans had been enslaved or killed.
key_events: Spanish slave raids depopulate the Bahamas by approximately 1520

930.name: Piracy, Privateering, and the Republic of Pirates
930.description: The Bahamas' uninhabited islands became a haven for pirates and privateers. Nassau emerged as the capital of the infamous 'Republic of Pirates,' home to Blackbeard, Charles Vane, and other notorious figures until Governor Woodes Rogers restored order.

sub_clusters.name: Eleutherian Adventurers and English Settlement
sub_clusters.description: English Puritans from Bermuda, known as the Eleutherian Adventurers, established the first permanent European settlement on the island they named Eleuthera in 1648, seeking religious freedom.
key_events: Eleutherian Adventurers settle Eleuthera in 1648

sub_clusters.name: Nassau and the Republic of Pirates
sub_clusters.description: Nassau became the de facto capital of piracy in the Caribbean. Blackbeard (Edward Teach), Charles Vane, Calico Jack Rackham, Anne Bonny, and Mary Read operated from Nassau. At its peak, over 1,000 pirates called Nassau home.
key_events: Blackbeard (Edward Teach) makes Nassau his base c. 1716
Governor Woodes Rogers arrives 1718 to suppress piracy
Charles Vane defies Rogers and escapes Nassau harbor

930.name: British Colonial Rule and Plantation Economy
930.description: After the suppression of piracy, the Bahamas became an established British colony. The arrival of American Loyalists after 1783 brought enslaved people and cotton plantation agriculture, transforming the islands' economy and demographics.

sub_clusters.name: Loyalist Settlement and Cotton Plantation Economy
sub_clusters.description: Following American independence, thousands of British Loyalists and their enslaved people relocated to the Bahamas, establishing cotton plantations on the Out Islands. This influx tripled the population and established a plantation-based slave economy.
key_events: Loyalist migration brings 7,000+ settlers and enslaved people 1783–1785
Cotton plantations established across the Out Islands

sub_clusters.name: Crown Colony Governance and Naval Operations
sub_clusters.description: The Bahamas functioned as a British Crown Colony with an appointed governor. The islands served as a strategic naval outpost, and wrecking (salvaging shipwrecks) became a major industry.

940.name: Emancipation and 19th-Century Transformation
940.description: The abolition of slavery, the transition to freedom, and the Bahamas' role in the American Civil War as a blockade-running hub that brought a brief economic boom to Nassau.

sub_clusters.name: Emancipation and the Emergence of Free Society
sub_clusters.description: The slave trade was abolished in 1807 and full emancipation came in 1834. The freed Black majority gradually established independent communities, while the white merchant elite (the 'Bay Street Boys') maintained economic and political control.
key_events: Full emancipation of enslaved people in 1834

sub_clusters.name: American Civil War Blockade Running
sub_clusters.description: Nassau experienced an economic boom as a hub for Confederate blockade runners during the American Civil War. Cotton was shipped out and war supplies smuggled back to the South, bringing enormous profits to Bahamian merchants.

950.name: Rum Running and Early 20th-Century Development
950.description: The Bahamas' proximity to the United States made it a major hub for liquor smuggling during American Prohibition, bringing a second windfall profit era. This period also saw the beginnings of the tourism industry and early political organizing.

sub_clusters.name: Prohibition-Era Rum Running
sub_clusters.description: During American Prohibition (1920–1933), the Bahamas became the primary staging ground for rum-running operations to the United States. Nassau warehouses stored vast quantities of liquor, and the trade enriched both Bahamian merchants and the colonial treasury.
key_events: Bahamas becomes major rum-running hub during US Prohibition 1920–1933
Nassau liquor warehouses fuel massive smuggling operations to Florida

sub_clusters.name: Early Tourism Development
sub_clusters.description: The emergence of tourism as an economic force, initially catering to wealthy American visitors. The Duke of Windsor served as governor during WWII (1940–1945), bringing international attention to the islands.

950.name: Majority Rule and Independence
950.description: The struggle for majority rule against the white-dominated 'Bay Street Boys,' the rise of Lynden Pindling and the Progressive Liberal Party, and the achievement of independence on July 10, 1973.

sub_clusters.name: Majority Rule and the End of Bay Street Dominance
sub_clusters.description: The Black majority's campaign for political equality against the white merchant oligarchy known as the 'Bay Street Boys.' Lynden Pindling led the Progressive Liberal Party (PLP) to victory in 1967, achieving majority rule.
key_events: Lynden Pindling wins majority rule for the PLP in 1967
Pindling throws the Speaker's mace out the window in dramatic 1965 protest

sub_clusters.name: Independence and Nation-Building
sub_clusters.description: The Bahamas achieved independence on July 10, 1973, with Lynden Pindling as Prime Minister. The nation developed its tourism and offshore banking sectors while navigating challenges including drug trafficking in the 1980s.
key_events: Independence of the Bahamas on July 10, 1973

960.name: Contemporary Bahamas
960.description: Modern Bahamas confronting climate change, hurricane vulnerability, economic dependence on tourism and finance, and the catastrophic impact of Hurricane Dorian in 2019.

sub_clusters.name: Offshore Banking and Economic Challenges
sub_clusters.description: The Bahamas' role as a major offshore financial center, facing increasing international pressure for transparency and regulatory compliance, alongside efforts to diversify the tourism-dependent economy.

sub_clusters.name: Hurricane Dorian Devastation
sub_clusters.description: Category 5 Hurricane Dorian struck the Abaco Islands and Grand Bahama on September 1, 2019, as the strongest Atlantic hurricane to make landfall. It stalled over the islands for over 40 hours, causing catastrophic destruction, killing at least 74 people, and leaving thousands homeless.
key_events: Hurricane Dorian strikes Abaco and Grand Bahama on September 1, 2019
Storm stalls for 40+ hours causing unprecedented destruction
Estimated $3.4 billion in damage — costliest disaster in Bahamian history

sub_clusters.name: Climate Vulnerability and Resilience Efforts
sub_clusters.description: As a low-lying archipelagic nation, the Bahamas faces existential threats from sea-level rise and intensifying hurricanes. The country has become a leading voice for small island developing states in international climate negotiations.

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
